newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open firm before jobless, orders.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open firm before jobless, orders.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher in New York on Friday, following gains in Tokyo built on the back of a firm dollar.
The market is anticipating friendly U.S. economic data this morning.
Weekly jobless claims, usually released on Thursday but postponed a day due to the Wednesday Christmas Day holiday, are expected to total 346,000, versus 351,000 a week earlier.
Durable goods orders for November are expected to be up a slight 0.1 percent, according to economists polled by Reuters.
Durable goods orders rose a modest 0.3 percent in October.
If the data come in as forecast, the market will see it as further evidence that the Federal Reserve has no near-term need to raise interest rates.
If the data deviate substantially from expectations, it could generate some volatility before the market settles back into a quieter, low volume trading session, analysts said.

In early trade before the data releases at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 4/32 to 99 even, yielding 6.58 percent. The highest yield for the T-bond on Thursday 6.59 percent. The lowest was 6.57 percent.

"We got a little firmness from the dollar overnight," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International "It climbed in Tokyo overnight. That gave us some support, but in a very thin market, however."
Rupert said she expects the market to stay close to unchanged in very thin trading.
"We might get a little more volatility early on, given the data this morning, but no sustainable moves," she said.
"The market is firm basically because the dollar is looking strong," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. "But the data could move the market if we get any surprises."
Surprises are not unusual when it comes to durable goods orders reports and the weekly jobless figures, Sloan noted.
"Durable goods and jobless claims are both volatile and quite often come in off (economists') expectations," he said.
Sloan looks for November durable goods orders to be up 0.5 percent. He anticipates a rise in jobless claims to 355,000 in the week ended December 21.
"The trend in jobless claims seems to be creeping upwards," said Sloan.
Sloan said the market got some support on Thursday from the Wall Street Journal's "subdued assessment of holiday shopping" strength.
"The market's bias is positive, mainly due to the strength in the dollar -- unless we get some upside shocks in the data," said Sloan. "The market should remain relatively quiet though."
In light trade, ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 101-7/32, yielding 6.33 percent.
Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 101-1/32, yielding 6.12 percent. Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-27/32, yielding 5.83 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down three basis points to 4.95 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.06 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.19 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
